extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, congressional staff, patent attorneys, patent stakeholders, and policy advocates interested in U.S. patent reform (H.R. 1249)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and review of legislative amendments and floor debate concerning H.R. 1249 (America Invents Act revisions), touching on first-inventor-to-file, tax-strategy patents, derivation proceedings, patent-term extensions, severability, and related PTO rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: No retroactive negation of patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing the law midstream fundamentally hurts applicants who disclosed and filed under the law in effect at the time; patent applications published and pending for years would be rendered useless and applicants would lose the ability to protect their innovations as trade secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative changes should not retroactively strip rights that applicants reasonably relied upon when deciding to disclose and pursue patents. Anti-pattern: applying new substantive exclusions or bans to already-published/pending applications without a protective carve-out. Example: applicants who disclosed code and how to make/use inventions under prior law would be unfairly penalized if law is changed to remove patentability for that subject matter after filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date for ban on tax strategy patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective date in the underlying bill applies to any patent application that is pending on, filed on or after, the date of enactment and to any patent that is issued on or after that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy choice: apply ban to pending applications (to prevent issuance of further tax-strategy patents) versus carve out pending applications (to avoid retroactive deprivation of rights). Supporters argue applying effective date to pending apps prevents further patents that could raise costs and complexity for taxpayers; opponents argue retroactive application is unfair to applicants who filed during a now-closed window. Considerations include fairness, administrative practicability, and public policy impact on taxpayers and tax-preparers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax strategy patents are bad public policy
rubrics_metrics.description: When one individual or business is given the exclusive right to a particular method of complying with the Tax Code, it increases the costs and complexity for every other citizen or tax preparer to comply with the Tax Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate patent policy against public-interest harms: patents that cover methods of complying with statutory obligations (e.g., tax compliance) can force taxpayers to choose between paying royalties or using inferior tax treatments. Anti-pattern: granting monopolies over ways to satisfy government mandates. Stakeholder consensus (AICPA, CPA caucus, CFP Board) cited as support for excluding tax-strategy patents from patentable subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify calculation of 60-day period for Hatch-Waxman patent term extension
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of determining the date on which a product receives permission under the second sentence (section 156(d)(1)), if such permission is transmitted after 4:30 P.M., Eastern Time, on a business day, or is transmitted on a day that is not a business day, the product shall be deemed to receive such permission on the next business day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical clarification removes ambiguity about deadlines, aligns PTO/FDA interpretations, and is intended to provide certainty to innovators investing in costly medical research. Example: consistent treatment with Medicines Co. v. Kappos. Anti-pattern: leaving conflicting agency interpretations unresolved, which may chill investment or produce inconsistent outcomes. Also consider separation-of-powers/process concerns when an amendment effectively resolves ongoing litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid legislative interference with ongoing litigation (special fixes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should not interfere with ongoing litigation by changing statutory language to affect a specific pending case (e.g., MedCo); such matters may be more appropriately handled through private relief bills or allowed to proceed through the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting statutory clarifications, weigh the benefits of legal certainty for all versus the risk of appearing to grant a special, case-specific remedy. Anti-pattern: enacting a provision that effectively fixes the outcome for a single company while litigation is pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation proceedings must be fair, reliable, and based on a solid record
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivation proceedings are a new process by which a party can defeat an earlier-filed patent application by showing that the invention in the earlier application was derived from the party’s invention or concept. The bill requires a party to support a petition for derivation by 'substantial evidence' to initiate a proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design derivation proceedings to balance access for true inventors with protection against speculative claims. Require rules for exchange of relevant information and evidence, permit rebuttal evidence, and ensure the Patent Office can decide on a complete evidentiary record. Anti-pattern: a petition-stage threshold so high that legitimate derivation claims (especially where inventor lacks direct documentary evidence) cannot be heard; or conversely, too low a threshold that invites frivolous proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require PTO rules for exchange of relevant information in derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment would require the PTO to provide rules for the exchange of relevant information by both parties, including requiring parties to provide sufficient evidence to prove and rebut a claim of derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rules should enable both sides to develop the factual record (discovery/exchange tailored to administrative setting) so the PTO can make informed determinations. Consider special evidentiary contexts (e.g., disclosures to intermediaries or venture capitalists) where direct documentary proof may be limited; allow mechanisms to link disclosures and downstream filings. Anti-pattern: leaving evidence exchange undeveloped, resulting in unfair outcomes or incomplete records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve/strengthen a 1-year grace period for disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill provides a stronger, more transparent and certain 1-year grace period for disclosures, protecting the ability of an inventor to discuss or write about their ideas for a patent up to 1 year before they file for patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace-period rules should be clear so inventors can rely on public disclosures without automatic forfeiture of rights. Implementation must define what qualifies as a disclosure, how it affects priority, and interaction with foreign filing strategies. Anti-pattern: ambiguous grace periods that generate priority disputes and uncertainty for small inventors and startups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application as a low-cost mechanism to preserve filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor submits an application to the Patent Office that describes their invention and how to make it; with a $110 fee this gets them a provisional application and preserves their filing date, allowing one year to complete the application while retaining the earlier filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional filings can be an affordable priority-preserving tool, but to be effective they must adequately describe the invention. Anti-pattern: filing minimal or low-quality provisionals that lack sufficient detail—good provisionals often require legal help and associated fees. Consider tradeoffs for small entities between provisional-filing costs and the costs of contested interference/derivation proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability clause to preserve remainder of the Act
rubrics_metrics.description: If any provision of this Act or amendment made by this Act, or the application of a provision or amendment to any person or circumstance, is held to be unconstitutional, the remainder of this Act and amendments shall not be affected by the holding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include standard severability language in legislation to prevent a single legal invalidation from voiding the entire statute. Anti-pattern: omitting severability provisions which risks greater disruption if part of the law is struck down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace interference proceedings with derivation in first-inventor-to-file regime
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill’s first-inventor-to-file provisions create a new 'derivation' process (replacing many functions of interference proceedings) to address situations where an earlier-filed application was derived from another inventor's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether derivation proceedings provide adequate protection for true inventors relative to prior interference practice. Consider costs, evidentiary standards, administrative capacity, and whether derivation is more or less favorable to independent inventors and small entities. Anti-pattern: creating a new administrative process without clear standards that inadvertently disadvantages particular classes of inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conforming statutory updates (rename BPAI to PTAB)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend sections of title 35 and related statutes to replace the term 'Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences' with 'Patent Trial and Appeal Board'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure cross-reference consistency across statutes when organizational or nomenclature changes are made. Administrative/ drafting criterion: comprehensively update statutory text to reflect new institutional structures. Anti-pattern: leaving inconsistent terminology that creates confusion about jurisdiction and processes.
